questions.domain: Secure, Optimize, and Deploy Database Solutions
questions.topic: Parameter Sniffing & OPTIMIZE FOR Query Hint
questions.codeSnippet:
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetOrdersByCustomer (@CustomerId INT)
AS
BEGIN
    SELECT OrderId, OrderDate, TotalAmount
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerId = @CustomerId
    OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@CustomerId = 1001));
END;
questions.stem: A stored procedure experiences erratic performance due to 'Parameter Sniffing': when compiled using a typical retail customer (5 orders), it produces an efficient Index Seek + Key Lookup plan. However, when compiled using the primary wholesale client (3 million orders), it produces an Index Scan plan that performs terribly for all other customers. You need the optimizer to consistently compile plans tailored to a typical retail customer without recompiling on every run. Which query hint should you apply?

options.text: OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@CustomerId = 1001))
options.rationale: The `OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR (@parameter = value))` hint directs the optimizer to compile the execution plan using the specified representative retail customer ID, stabilizing the plan across subsequent executions without per-invocation recompilations.

options.text: OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN)
options.rationale: OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN utilizes table-wide average statistical density rather than optimizing for a specific typical customer profile.

options.text: OPTION (RECOMPILE, USE HINT('DISABLE_PARAMETER_SNIFFING'))
options.rationale: OPTION (RECOMPILE) forces CPU-intensive compilation on every execution, violating the requirement to avoid per-run recompilations.

options.text: OPTION (KEEPFIXED PLAN, FORCE ORDER)
options.rationale: KEEPFIXED PLAN prevents recompilation due to statistics updates, but locks in the sub-optimal plan if initial compilation occurred with the wholesale customer.

questions.explanation: Parameter Sniffing occurs when SQL Server optimizes a procedure using the parameter value provided during initial compilation. `OPTIMIZE FOR (@variable = value)` stabilizes the plan so it reflects the expected representative data distribution rather than being dictated by whichever parameter invoked the initial compilation.

theoryPill.title: Mitigating Parameter Sniffing in T-SQL
theoryPill.summary: Stabilizing execution plans for queries over skewed data distributions.
keyPoints: OPTIMIZE FOR (@var = val): Compiles the plan optimized for a specific high-frequency literal value.
OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN: Uses average histogram density instead of sniffing incoming parameter values.
OPTION (RECOMPILE): Forces plan recompilation on each run (useful for infrequent or highly complex queries).
Local variables: Assigning parameters to local variables within procedures forces average density estimates.
theoryPill.examTrap: OPTION (RECOMPILE) carries CPU compilation cost on every invocation; for procedures called thousands of times per second, OPTIMIZE FOR is significantly more efficient.

questions.topic: Concurrency - Read Committed Snapshot Isolation (RCSI)
questions.codeSnippet:
ALTER DATABASE SalesDB
SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;
questions.stem: In a high-concurrency OLTP database, analytical reporting read queries cause severe blocking and deadlocks against order insert and update transactions. You need to eliminate blocking between readers and writers without permitting dirty reads and without modifying any application T-SQL queries. What database-level configuration should you enable?

options.text: ALTER DATABASE SalesDB SET READ_COMMITTED_SNAPSHOT ON;
options.rationale: Read Committed Snapshot Isolation (RCSI) uses row versioning in TempDB transparently under standard READ COMMITTED, preventing readers from acquiring shared (S) locks without requiring changes to application T-SQL code.

options.text: ALTER DATABASE SalesDB SET ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION ON;
options.rationale: ALLOW_SNAPSHOT_ISOLATION enables snapshot isolation, but requires modifying client code to issue SET TRANSACTION ISOLATION LEVEL SNAPSHOT in each session.

options.text: ALTER DATABASE SalesDB SET MEMORY_OPTIMIZED_ELEVATE_TO_SNAPSHOT = ON;
options.rationale: MEMORY_OPTIMIZED_ELEVATE_TO_SNAPSHOT applies only to In-Memory OLTP tables and does not affect disk-based tables.

options.text: ALTER DATABASE SalesDB SET DELAYED_DURABILITY = FORCED;
options.rationale: DELAYED_DURABILITY flushes the transaction log asynchronously, but does not eliminate shared and exclusive locking contention.

questions.explanation: Read Committed Snapshot Isolation (RCSI) is the recommended concurrency setting in Azure SQL Database (enabled by default) and SQL Server for high-concurrency workloads. Readers access committed historical row versions in TempDB without acquiring shared locks that block writers.

theoryPill.title: Row Versioning Concurrency Control (RCSI)
theoryPill.summary: Eliminating reader-writer blocking while ensuring transactional consistency.
keyPoints: Core principle: Writers do not block readers; readers do not block writers.
Mechanism: Maintains committed historical row versions in the TempDB Version Store.
Transparency: Operates under the default READ COMMITTED isolation level without code changes.
Consideration: Sizing TempDB properly to support row version volume.
theoryPill.examTrap: In Azure SQL Database, RCSI is enabled ON by default; in on-premises SQL Server it defaults to OFF.

questions.explanation: The `system_health` Extended Events session runs automatically in the background on SQL Server and Azure SQL. xml_deadlock_report event: Details victim-list, process-list, and resource-list XML nodes.

options.rationale: A SQL Database Project compiled into a DACPAC declaratively defines the target schema; SqlPackage compares the model against the target database, generates an incremental differential script, and enforces safety checks against accidental data loss.

FROM dbo.Employees
FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF '2025-06-01 12:00:00'

questions.stem: Due to compliance requirements, you must preserve an immutable audit history of all employee salary changes over time, allowing queries to inspect what salary an employee earned at any arbitrary historical timestamp ('time travel'). What native T-SQL capability should you implement on the table?

options.text: System-versioned temporal tables (SYSTEM_VERSIONING = ON) with DATETIME2 period columns PERIOD FOR SYSTEM_TIME and FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF queries.
options.rationale: System-versioned temporal tables automatically archive previous row states into a system-managed history table, enabling historical reconstruction at any point in time using `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`.

options.text: Change Tracking configured with CHANGE_RETENTION = 365 DAYS queried via CHANGETABLE(CHANGES dbo.Employees, @version).
options.rationale: Change Tracking only tracks changed primary keys and versions for synchronization, without preserving historical column values.

options.text: Append-only Ledger tables (LEDGER = ON (APPEND_ONLY = ON)) prohibiting UPDATE statements on the employee table.
options.rationale: Append-only ledger tables prohibit UPDATE statements entirely; updatable tables with history require system versioning.

options.text: Hourly database snapshots (CREATE DATABASE ... AS SNAPSHOT OF) scheduled via SQL Agent jobs to retain data pages.
options.rationale: Database snapshots do not provide point-in-time querying via FOR SYSTEM_TIME and degrade write throughput when multiplied.

questions.explanation: **System-versioned temporal tables** manage two physical tables: the current table and the history table. When rows are updated or deleted, the database engine archives previous versions with UTC timestamps, enabling time-travel queries via `FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`.

questions.stem: In a table containing 50 million historical rows, 99% of orders have `Status = 'Completed'` and only 1% have `Status = 'Pending'`. Warehouse operators continuously query pending orders by date and customer. You need these queries to return in milliseconds while minimizing storage footprint and index maintenance overhead during bulk inserts. Which indexing strategy represents best practice?

options.text: A filtered nonclustered index (CREATE NONCLUSTERED INDEX ... WHERE Status = 'Pending') on columns (OrderDate, CustomerId).
options.rationale: A filtered index covers only the 1% of rows matching `Status = 'Pending'`, reducing index storage by 99% and eliminating index maintenance overhead when orders transition to 'Completed'.

options.text: An unfiltered nonclustered columnstore index (NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX) over (Status, OrderDate, CustomerId).
options.rationale: Columnstore indexes optimize analytical scans and aggregations, but add overhead to transactional point lookups and store all 50 million rows.

options.text: A composite clustered index (CLUSTERED INDEX) defined on (Status ASC, OrderDate DESC) with PAGE data compression.
options.rationale: Clustering by a volatile low-cardinality status column causes expensive physical row relocations whenever order statuses change.

options.text: A standard nonclustered index on (Status, OrderDate) including all table columns in the INCLUDE list with FILLFACTOR = 50.
options.rationale: An unfiltered nonclustered index indexes the 99% completed rows needlessly and reserving 50% empty space multiplies disk and memory consumption.

questions.explanation: **Filtered Indexes** use a `WHERE` predicate to index only a specific subset of table rows. They are ideal for skewed columns where queries filter against infrequent values, such as pending work queues or non-null attributes.

questions.topic: Row-Level Security - Filter vs Block Predicates
questions.codeSnippet:
CREATE SECURITY POLICY SalesFilter
ADD FILTER PREDICATE Security.fn_securitypredicate(SalesTerritory) ON dbo.Orders,
ADD BLOCK PREDICATE Security.fn_securitypredicate(SalesTerritory) ON dbo.Orders AFTER UPDATE
WITH (STATE = ON);
questions.stem: In a Row-Level Security policy, what is the technical difference between a FILTER PREDICATE and a BLOCK PREDICATE AFTER UPDATE?

options.text: FILTER PREDICATE silently filters out rows during read operations (SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE), whereas BLOCK PREDICATE AFTER UPDATE aborts the transaction with an error if an updated value violates the predicate.
options.rationale: A FILTER predicate silently conceals rows not permitted to the user without raising errors. A BLOCK predicate AFTER UPDATE validates the new state of a modified row and aborts the statement if a user attempts to update a row into an unauthorized territory.

options.text: FILTER PREDICATE blocks INSERT operations of rows outside the user's scope, whereas BLOCK PREDICATE AFTER UPDATE silently hides rows in SELECT queries without errors.
options.rationale: This reverses the concepts: FILTER predicates do not block inserts (blocking inserts requires BLOCK PREDICATE AFTER INSERT), and BLOCK predicates do not filter SELECT statements.

options.text: FILTER PREDICATE evaluates before modifying rows on disk (BEFORE UPDATE), whereas BLOCK PREDICATE AFTER UPDATE only applies visual masking on updated columns.
options.rationale: Evaluating before modification is handled by BLOCK PREDICATE BEFORE UPDATE, and RLS predicates do not perform column data masking.

options.text: Both predicates reject queries with permission error 229 when encountering rows from other territories, but BLOCK PREDICATE AFTER UPDATE rolls back the entire session.
options.rationale: FILTER predicates never produce permission error 229; they silently exclude non-permitted rows from the query result set.

questions.explanation: Row-Level Security combines `FILTER PREDICATE` (silently restricts row visibility on read operations) and `BLOCK PREDICATE` (blocks unauthorized INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE attempts by throwing exceptions).

theoryPill.title: Predicates in Row-Level Security (RLS)
theoryPill.summary: Read governance (FILTER) and mutation enforcement (BLOCK) in T-SQL tables.
keyPoints: FILTER PREDICATE: Filters rows during SELECT, UPDATE, and DELETE; unauthorized rows do not appear in result sets.
BLOCK PREDICATE BEFORE/AFTER: Rejects unauthorized INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE attempts with a security violation error.
Inline Table-Valued Function: Predicate logic must be written as an inline TVF for optimal query plan inlining.
theoryPill.examTrap: Without a BLOCK PREDICATE, a user could update an accessible row and reassign it to another client or department, losing visibility but successfully altering the data.

questions.topic: Index Defragmentation - REORGANIZE vs REBUILD
questions.stem: During routine database maintenance, you inspect `sys.dm_db_index_physical_stats`. The clustered index on an 80 GB primary table exhibits 18% external logical fragmentation. You must reduce fragmentation with minimal resource overhead, without locking user queries, and without requiring extra disk space in TempDB. Following standard Microsoft recommendations, which action should you execute?

options.text: ALTER INDEX ALL ON dbo.MainTable REORGANIZE;
options.rationale: For moderate fragmentation between 5% and 30% (18%), Microsoft best practice recommends REORGANIZE because it compacts leaf-level pages online without exclusive table locks or TempDB space requirements.

options.text: ALTER INDEX ALL ON dbo.MainTable REBUILD WITH (ONLINE = OFF, SORT_IN_TEMPDB = ON);
options.rationale: REBUILD with ONLINE = OFF locks user queries, and SORT_IN_TEMPDB = ON requires extra disk space in TempDB, violating both scenario constraints.

options.text: DBCC INDEXDEFRAG (0, 'dbo.MainTable', 1) WITH NO_INFOMSGS;
options.rationale: DBCC INDEXDEFRAG is a deprecated command replaced by ALTER INDEX ... REORGANIZE.

options.text: UPDATE STATISTICS dbo.MainTable WITH FULLSCAN, NORECOMPUTE;
options.rationale: UPDATE STATISTICS recalculates distribution histograms for the query optimizer, but does not physically reorganize index pages or remove index fragmentation.

questions.explanation: Microsoft index defragmentation guidelines: fragmentation < 5% = do nothing; 5% to 30% = `ALTER INDEX REORGANIZE`; > 30% = `ALTER INDEX REBUILD`.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company must track the chain of custody for clinical trials in Azure SQL Database. Regulatory rules mandate that no row in the results table may be altered or deleted—even by a Global Administrator with DBA privileges—and that any tampering attempt must be cryptographically verifiable. options.rationale: Append-Only Ledger Tables block UPDATE and DELETE statements at the database engine level even for sysadmin DBAs, chaining row transactions with SHA-256 hashes in verifiable database digests.

questions.stem: When analyzing the execution plan of a query sorting 20 million rows, you observe a yellow warning icon stating 'Sort spill to TempDB'. What is the technical cause of this warning and how is it mitigated?

options.text: Cardinality estimation under-allocated memory, causing Sort to spill data to TempDB; mitigated by updating statistics or enabling Memory Grant Feedback.
options.rationale: A 'Sort spill to TempDB' occurs when the Sort operator receives more rows than estimated, exhausting its assigned Memory Grant and spilling intermediate sorted runs to disk in TempDB.

options.text: The buffer pool reached clean page limits due to a CHECKPOINT event; mitigated by reducing parallelism using OPTION (MAXDOP 1) on the database.
options.rationale: CHECKPOINT operations flush dirty pages to disk, but do not produce sort spill warnings on query execution operators.

options.text: The query lacks explicit locking hints and experiences PAGELATCH_EX contention on PFS allocation pages; mitigated using WITH (NOLOCK) on tables.
options.rationale: WITH (NOLOCK) changes transaction isolation to READ UNCOMMITTED, but does not increase query memory grants or eliminate sort spills.

options.text: The primary database transaction log became full during read-only sorting; mitigated by changing the recovery model from FULL to SIMPLE.
options.rationale: A read-only SELECT query uses workspace in TempDB when sorting, not transaction log space in the user database.

questions.explanation: When granted memory is inadequate to sort result sets entirely in RAM, the database engine spills intermediate data to TempDB on disk, severely impacting query latency.

questions.stem: In `sys.dm_os_wait_stats`, the dominant wait type observed on the server is 'PAGEIOLATCH_SH'. Which physical subsystem bottleneck is indicated by this wait statistic?

options.text: Waiting on physical disk I/O reads transferring data pages from storage into the memory Buffer Pool (caused by table scans, missing indexes, or memory pressure).
options.rationale: PAGEIOLATCH_SH occurs when a worker thread requests a data page not present in the buffer pool and must wait while storage subsystem reads bring the page from disk into memory.

options.text: Memory RAM contention on allocation map pages (PFS, GAM, SGAM) in TempDB caused by rapid creation and destruction of temporary tables.
options.rationale: In-memory page latch contention on already-loaded pages is recorded as PAGELATCH_UP or PAGELATCH_EX (without the 'IO' designation).

options.text: Logical transaction lock blocking where reader sessions wait for another transaction to release an exclusive (X) lock on a modified row.
options.rationale: Transactional blocking waits are categorized under LCK_M_S, LCK_M_U, or LCK_M_X, not physical I/O latches.

options.text: Network saturation when transmitting massive query result sets to a client application consuming rows slowly row-by-row.
options.rationale: Slow client consumption or network transfer latency is tracked under the ASYNC_NETWORK_IO wait type.

questions.explanation: PAGEIOLATCH_SH indicates that a thread is blocked waiting for physical disk reads to fetch requested pages into the memory buffer cache.

questions.stem: In a T-SQL query evaluating `VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', @v1, EmbeddingCol)`, what is the database engine behavior if `EmbeddingCol` contains a NULL value for a specific row?

options.text: The VECTOR_DISTANCE function evaluates to NULL for that row without aborting the query, adhering to ANSI SQL three-valued logic.
options.rationale: In T-SQL, if either argument passed to VECTOR_DISTANCE is NULL, the function returns NULL; since NULL values sort first in ascending ORDER BY, a WHERE EmbeddingCol IS NOT NULL filter is required.

options.text: The engine implicitly replaces the NULL value with a zero vector (0.0 across all dimensions) and returns a cosine distance of 1.0.
options.rationale: SQL Server never converts a NULL vector into an all-zero vector, and an all-zero vector has undefined direction under cosine distance.

options.text: The entire SELECT statement fails immediately with runtime error 8134 (divide-by-zero error) and terminates the active transaction.
options.rationale: A NULL value in a vector column does not throw a query-terminating exception; the scalar expression simply evaluates to NULL.

options.text: The function returns the maximum floating-point value (1.79E+308) to ensure rows with NULL vectors appear last in the result set.
options.rationale: VECTOR_DISTANCE returns NULL (not 1.79E+308), and in T-SQL NULL values sort as the lowest possible values in ORDER BY ... ASC.

questions.explanation: In accordance with SQL three-valued logic, passing a NULL operand to the VECTOR_DISTANCE scalar function yields NULL without terminating the query.

theoryPill.title: NULL Handling and Zero-Magnitude Vectors in VECTOR_DISTANCE
theoryPill.summary: Critical implications of `ORDER BY ... ASC` when vector columns allow NULL values.
keyPoints: NULL propagation: If either input vector (`@v1` or `EmbeddingCol`) is `NULL`, `VECTOR_DISTANCE` returns `NULL`.

T-SQL sorting behavior: In SQL Server and Azure SQL, `NULL` values sort **first** in `ORDER BY DistanceScore ASC`. Therefore, `SELECT TOP 5 ... ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE(...) ASC` will return `NULL` rows before nearest matches unless you specify `WHERE EmbeddingCol IS NOT NULL`.
Zero-magnitude vectors `[0, 0, ...]`: In `'cosine'` metric mode, an all-zero vector has zero magnitude and undefined angle, causing `VECTOR_DISTANCE('cosine', ...)` to return `NULL`.
theoryPill.examTrap: When querying a nullable `VECTOR(d)` column with `TOP N ... ORDER BY VECTOR_DISTANCE(...) ASC`, always include `WHERE EmbeddingCol IS NOT NULL` to avoid NULL values occupying top ranks.

questions.topic: Database CI/CD - Schema Compare in Visual Studio / VS Code
questions.stem: When working with SQL Database Projects (.sqlproj), a developer needs to visually compare schema differences between a local Git project and a live test database to generate an incremental deployment script. Which integrated tooling provides this capability?

options.text: Schema Compare in the SQL Database Projects extension for VS Code / Visual Studio, or the Script/Publish action in SqlPackage.
options.rationale: Schema Compare inspects the object model of a .sqlproj project or DACPAC against a target live database, highlights object-level differences, and generates the incremental synchronization DDL script.

options.text: The sp_BlitzDiff system stored procedure executed inside a SQL Server Profiler trace capture session.
options.rationale: SQL Server Profiler is a legacy performance trace capture tool and does not provide schema differential comparison against Git project models.

options.text: The tablediff.exe command-line utility invoked directly against the .sql source files in the local Git repository.
options.rationale: tablediff.exe compares table row data between two live tables for replication troubleshooting, not declarative schema definitions from a .sqlproj project.

options.text: The DBCC CHECKCATALOG command executed with the WITH ESTIMATEONLY option against the target test database.
options.rationale: DBCC CHECKCATALOG verifies system catalog consistency within a single database; it does not perform differential schema comparisons against external projects.

questions.explanation: Schema Compare analyzes source and target database definitions, highlights differences, and creates an incremental deployment script to synchronize them.

theoryPill.title: Schema Compare and Workflows with SQL Database Projects (.sqlproj)
theoryPill.summary: Declarative schema synchronization and change inspection between source control and databases.
keyPoints: Supported sources and targets: Allows comparison between any combination of live Databases, `.sqlproj` projects, and compiled `.dacpac` files.
Interface capabilities: Allows developers to include or exclude specific objects (tables, views, procedures), apply changes directly, or export the incremental `.sql` script.
CLI automation: In CI/CD pipelines, `SqlPackage /Action:Script` or `/Action:DeployReport` generates the identical differential analysis non-interactively.
theoryPill.examTrap: Do not confuse `Schema Compare` (which compares DDL object definitions) with `tablediff.exe` or `Data Compare` (which compare data rows stored inside tables).

questions.topic: Database Migration - Azure Database Migration Service (DMS)
questions.stem: To migrate an on-premises 10 TB SQL Server database to Azure SQL Managed Instance with near-zero downtime, which managed Microsoft migration tooling should you use?

options.text: Azure Database Migration Service (DMS) or the Azure SQL Migration extension in online migration mode with continuous transaction log shipping.
options.rationale: Online migration via Azure DMS or the Azure SQL Migration extension restores an initial full backup and continuously replays transaction logs until final cutover with minimal application downtime.

options.text: Exporting a BACPAC file using SqlPackage Export and importing it into Azure SQL Managed Instance from Azure Blob Storage.
options.rationale: Exporting and importing a BACPAC file for a 10 TB database would take multiple days and requires halting source writes, violating the near-zero downtime requirement.

options.text: The SSMS Generate and Publish Scripts Wizard configured with the 'Types of data to script = Schema and data' option.
options.rationale: Generating plain-text INSERT script files for 10 TB of data is completely unviable and would produce multi-terabyte script files impossible to execute online.

options.text: Bulk copying via bcp.exe executed table-by-table without disabling triggers or foreign keys during a scheduled maintenance window.
options.rationale: Executing bcp table by table across 10 TB does not synchronize ongoing transactional changes and fails to migrate instance-level security logins and agent jobs.

questions.explanation: Azure DMS in online migration mode continuously synchronizes ongoing transactions via transaction log backups until the final cutover, enabling near-zero downtime for large databases.

theoryPill.title: Migration Strategies to Azure SQL Managed Instance (Online vs. Offline)
theoryPill.summary: Tool selection for high-volume database migrations requiring minimal downtime.
keyPoints: Azure SQL Migration / DMS (Online Mode): Restores a baseline full backup and continuously applies transaction log backups from Azure Blob Storage until cutover.
Managed Instance Link (MI Link): Employs Distributed Availability Groups to replicate data in near-real-time between SQL Server and Azure SQL MI, enabling instantaneous cutover.
Native Backup and Restore (`RESTORE DATABASE ... FROM URL`): Ideal for offline migrations, but requires downtime during the final differential and log restore window.
theoryPill.examTrap: Never choose BACPAC export/import for multi-terabyte databases or scenarios requiring near-zero downtime; BACPAC is strictly for logical schema and small dataset migrations.

questions.topic: T-SQL Window Functions - DENSE_RANK vs RANK
questions.stem: In an analytical query ranking customers by revenue, two customers share the identical purchase volume and tie for rank 2. You require the next customer in sequence to be assigned rank 3 without leaving any gaps in the numbering sequence. Which window function should you use?

options.text: DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY TotalFacturacion DESC).
options.rationale: DENSE_RANK() assigns the same rank to tied values and advances to the immediate consecutive integer without leaving gaps in the sequence (1, 2, 2, 3).

options.text: RANK() OVER (ORDER BY TotalFacturacion DESC).
options.rationale: RANK() assigns rank 2 to both tied customers but skips numbers equal to the tie count, producing a sequence with gaps (1, 2, 2, 4).

options.text: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY TotalFacturacion DESC).
options.rationale: ROW_NUMBER() assigns strictly distinct sequential numbers without acknowledging ties, non-deterministically ranking the tied customers as 2 and 3 (1, 2, 3, 4).

options.text: NTILE(3) OVER (ORDER BY TotalFacturacion DESC).
options.rationale: NTILE(3) divides rows into 3 equal-sized buckets (tertiles) rather than computing individual ranking positions based on ordered revenue values.

questions.explanation: DENSE_RANK does not produce gaps in rank values following tied positions (yielding 1, 2, 2, 3), whereas RANK produces gaps (yielding 1, 2, 2, 4).

theoryPill.title: T-SQL Window Ranking Functions: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, and NTILE
theoryPill.summary: Precise behavior when ties occur within the `ORDER BY` evaluation clause.
keyPoints: ROW_NUMBER(): Assigns a unique sequential integer starting from 1 with no ties: `1, 2, 3, 4`.
RANK(): Assigns identical rank values to ties, but skips values corresponding to the number of tied rows: `1, 2, 2, 4`.
DENSE_RANK(): Assigns identical rank values to ties, WITHOUT skipping any numbers in the subsequent sequence: `1, 2, 2, 3`.
NTILE(n): Distributes rows across `n` ordered buckets numbered 1 through `n`.
theoryPill.examTrap: If a question requires tied rows to receive the same rank and the subsequent row to receive the immediately following integer without gaps, the correct answer is always `DENSE_RANK()`.

questions.topic: Recursive CTE for Hierarchical Organization Trees
questions.stem: In a Human Resources database, you need to traverse upward through an employee's entire reporting chain of command up to the Chief Executive Officer (CEO). Which T-SQL construct is the most efficient declarative method to query hierarchical tree structures?

options.text: A recursive common table expression (Recursive CTE) composed of an anchor member and a recursive member joined by the UNION ALL operator.
options.rationale: A recursive CTE in T-SQL executes an anchor query (initial employee) and iteratively applies the recursive member joined via UNION ALL (e.ManagerID = cte.EmployeeID) until the hierarchy root is reached.

options.text: A recursive common table expression (Recursive CTE) where the anchor member and recursive member are combined using UNION (distinct) or INTERSECT.
options.rationale: In T-SQL, recursive CTE definitions strictly require the UNION ALL operator; combining anchor and recursive members using UNION or INTERSECT causes a compilation error.

options.text: A single-level SELECT query combining LAG(ManagerID) and LEAD(ManagerID) window functions partitioned by DepartmentID.
options.rationale: LAG and LEAD only access rows at a fixed offset within an ordered partition; they cannot iteratively traverse parent-child hierarchies of arbitrary depth.

options.text: A correlated subquery using the CROSS APPLY operator that invokes itself by name within the outer query WHERE clause.
options.rationale: A subquery or derived table in CROSS APPLY cannot reference its own alias recursively; recursive self-referencing requires a CTE.

questions.explanation: A recursive CTE defines an anchor member and a recursive member joined by UNION ALL to traverse hierarchical data structures efficiently without procedural cursors.

theoryPill.title: Structure and Rules of Recursive CTEs in T-SQL
theoryPill.summary: Declarative traversal of parent-child hierarchies (organizational charts, bill of materials).
keyPoints: Anchor member: Non-recursive query that returns the starting base row(s) or root node.
Mandatory operator: The anchor member and recursive member must be combined using `UNION ALL`.
Recursive member: References the CTE itself exactly once and terminates automatically when an iteration produces zero rows.
Recursion control: The `OPTION (MAXRECURSION n)` query hint (default 100; `0` = unlimited) protects against infinite loops caused by cyclic data.
theoryPill.examTrap: Using `UNION` (instead of `UNION ALL`), outer joins to the recursive CTE, `GROUP BY`, or `TOP` inside the recursive member is prohibited by the T-SQL compiler.

questions.topic: JSON_MODIFY for In-Place JSON Updates
questions.stem: You need to update a telephone number property within a JSON document stored in an NVARCHAR(MAX) column without rewriting the entire document or parsing it in external application code. Which T-SQL function updates a specific property in place?

options.text: UPDATE dbo.Customers SET ProfileJson = JSON_MODIFY(ProfileJson, '$.contacto.telefono', @NuevoTelefono) WHERE CustomerId = @Id;
options.rationale: JSON_MODIFY navigates to the specified JSON path ('$.contacto.telefono'), replaces the scalar value with @NuevoTelefono, and returns the modified JSON document.

options.text: UPDATE dbo.Customers SET ProfileJson = JSON_VALUE(ProfileJson, '$.contacto.telefono', @NuevoTelefono) WHERE CustomerId = @Id;
options.rationale: JSON_VALUE is a read-only scalar extraction function that accepts only two parameters (document and path); it cannot modify JSON content.

options.text: UPDATE dbo.Customers SET ProfileJson = JSON_QUERY(ProfileJson, 'append $.contacto.telefono', @NuevoTelefono) WHERE CustomerId = @Id;
options.rationale: JSON_QUERY only extracts JSON objects or arrays from an existing string; it does not perform in-place updates or accept a replacement value.

options.text: UPDATE dbo.Customers SET ProfileJson.modify('replace value of (/contacto/telefono)[1] with sql:variable("@NuevoTelefono")') WHERE CustomerId = @Id;
options.rationale: The .modify() XML DML method is exclusive to the XML data type and produces syntax errors when invoked against JSON stored in NVARCHAR(MAX).

questions.explanation: JSON_MODIFY updates the value of a property or array element in a JSON string and returns the updated JSON document while leaving the remainder unchanged.

theoryPill.title: Modifying JSON Documents in T-SQL with JSON_MODIFY
theoryPill.summary: In-place property updates, array appending, and key deletions in JSON strings.
keyPoints: Update or insert property: `JSON_MODIFY(@json, '$.path.property', 'NewValue')` updates the property if it exists or creates it if absent (in default lax mode).
Append to array: `JSON_MODIFY(@json, 'append $.tags', 'NewTag')` inserts a new element at the end of the specified JSON array.
Delete property: `JSON_MODIFY(@json, '$.path.property', NULL)` in `lax` mode removes the key entirely from the JSON object; in `strict` mode it sets the property to literal `null`.
Insert unescaped JSON sub-objects: Pass the replacement object wrapped inside `JSON_QUERY(@subJson)` to prevent T-SQL from escaping quotes as plain text.
theoryPill.examTrap: If you pass a JSON string as the third parameter to `JSON_MODIFY` without wrapping it in `JSON_QUERY()`, the engine escapes quotes and stores it as a literal string rather than an embedded JSON object.

questions.topic: Responsible AI in Database Engineering - Bias & Data Drift
questions.stem: An analytical database feeds credit-scoring predictive machine learning models. Over several years, consumer spending habits change significantly, causing model accuracy to degrade (Data Drift). Which database engineering practice should you implement to detect this phenomenon proactively?

options.text: Implement automated data profiling procedures that periodically compare current feature distributions, means, and quartiles against the training baseline.
options.rationale: Detecting Data Drift in the data tier requires continuous monitoring of statistical column distributions (means, standard deviations, histograms, or population stability index) against baseline training data.

options.text: Enable automatic plan correction in Query Store (FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN = ON) to prevent inference queries from modifying their physical disk access plans.
options.rationale: FORCE_LAST_GOOD_PLAN resolves query optimizer plan regressions; it has no insight into statistical shifts in underlying business data distributions.

options.text: Configure SERIALIZABLE transaction isolation and enable Transparent Data Encryption (TDE) across all feature store database tables.
options.rationale: SERIALIZABLE isolation and TDE protect concurrency and data at rest; they do not monitor or alert on statistical drift in feature values over time.

options.text: Permanently freeze database statistics by executing ALTER DATABASE CURRENT SET AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS OFF on all tables feeding the model.
options.rationale: Disabling AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS leads to poor query execution plans and hides underlying data distribution changes rather than detecting Data Drift.

questions.explanation: Data drift is detected by continuously profiling the statistical distribution of incoming production features and comparing them against baseline training datasets.

theoryPill.title: Data Governance for Responsible AI: Detecting Data Drift and Bias in SQL
theoryPill.summary: Database engineering practices to ensure reliability, fairness, and compliance in AI solutions.
keyPoints: Data Drift: Occurs when the statistical distribution of live operational data diverges from the historical data used to train the machine learning model.
T-SQL monitoring: Utilizing statistical aggregations (`AVG`, `STDEV`, `VAR`, `PERCENTILE_CONT`), null counts, and distribution metrics over rolling time windows to trigger retraining workflows.

Reproducibility with Temporal Tables: System-Versioned Temporal Tables (`FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`) enable point-in-time feature reconstruction as of the exact prediction timestamp for Responsible AI audits.
theoryPill.examTrap: To audit the exact historical feature values used to generate an AI prediction 6 months ago, System-Versioned Temporal Tables (`FOR SYSTEM_TIME AS OF`) provide native, tamper-resistant reproducibility.
